Uranus. The seventh planet from the Sun, an ice giant made of water, methane, and ammonia ices wrapped around a rocky core, rotated nearly ninety degrees on its side, likely from an ancient collision, and home to the coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system. Named after the Greek god of the sky, it was the first planet discovered in the modern era.

William Herschel discovered it in seventeen eighty-one. For two thousand years before that, astronomers had known no planets beyond Saturn. The discovery instantly doubled the known size of the solar system and forever changed humanity's conception of the cosmos. Uranus appears as a featureless blue-green disc because methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light while reflecting blue and green wavelengths, giving it that distinctive cyan hue.

The planet rotates at an extreme ninety-eight-degree axial tilt, meaning it essentially orbits the Sun on its side. Scientists believe a collision with a large body early in solar system history, possibly even a planet-mass object, knocked it sideways. The methane, ammonia, and water ices that compose it, surrounding a small rocky core, place it in its own category apart from Jupiter and Saturn, the gas giants that lack solid surfaces.

A year on Uranus takes eighty-four Earth years to complete, making it among the slowest-orbiting planets we can observe from Earth. That means a year on Uranus lasts nearly a human lifetime. The discovery itself was mathematically predicted by Urbain Le Verrier based on orbital wobbles detected in Neptune's path, a triumph of celestial mechanics and Newton's laws.

The planet has twenty-seven known moons and a subtle ring system. The five largest moons—Titania, Oberon, Umbriel, Ariel, and Miranda—display remarkably diverse geological features that the Voyager 2 probe revealed during its historic nineteen eighty-six flyby. Perhaps most strikingly, Uranus possesses the fastest wind speeds in the solar system, with atmospheric winds reaching up to nine hundred kilometers per hour. This is surprising given its distant location and minimal solar heating. Even more puzzling, Uranus emits more heat than it receives from the Sun, an anomaly suggesting internal energy from planetary compression and cooling since its formation.

Neptune, the outer ice giant, shares with Uranus the connection that its orbital perturbations led to Uranus's discovery. Saturn and Jupiter, fellow giants with their own ring systems and multiple moons, sit alongside Uranus in the solar system, which is the planetary system within which Uranus orbits. The NASA agency conducted modern exploration of Uranus via the Voyager 2 probe's historic flyby.
